title: Bigsky inquest wraps up
subtitle: Mother feels he was wrongly killed, that justice not done: lawyer
article: The family of Melvin Bigsky took little comfort from a set of 11 recommendations delivered by a coroner's inquest Monday.

His mother Christina, whose anguish was plain last week as witnesses described the graphic details of his shooting death by RCMP Const. James Flack, had planned to give a statement to reporters after the six-member jury completed its task.
But when the time came, it was just too difficult for her, the family's lawyer said outside court.
"Christina is very clear on this. She thinks her son was wrongly killed and her view is that an individual officer is essentially going unpunished, undisciplined, for it," Ron Piche said.

"She sees things as black and white as that. These recommendations don't really touch on that issue, they look forward somewhat to the bigger issue -- how do police conduct themselves, and are there areas that we can target to help avoid this situation in the future?"

Melvin Bigsky died of a single gunshot wound to the head at about 9 p.m. on April 27, 2001. The bullet was fired after a harrowing confrontation that unfolded quickly after Flack, acting on a report of a drunk driver, pulled over a truck in which Bigsky was a passenger.

During the struggle, Flack used both pepper spray and a baton against Bigsky with little effect. The officer was punched twice in the face, and Bigsky drove the truck into his cruiser, disabling it in the ditch.

Flack told the inquest his actions were based on his RCMP training regarding escalation of force, and that he believed Bigsky was trying to kill him with the truck, which had become stuck in the ditch. He does not face any criminal charges in connection with the death.

Under directions from presiding coroner Doug Kovatch, the six- member jury found Bigsky met his death by means of homicide, though that finding does not imply any criminal or civil responsibility under the Coroner's Act -- it simply means his death was caused by another person.

After deliberating for about six hours, the jury recommended a number of changes to police procedure, including installation of video cameras inside patrol cars, a requirement that drivers be ordered to drop their car keys out the window when stopped by police, abolishing the practice of sending officers on patrol alone, and having at least one aboriginal person at every RCMP detachment.
The jury also recommended that the public be encouraged to co- operate with police when they are pulled over -- though doing otherwise is already a criminal offence.

Bruce Gibson, the lawyer representing the RCMP during the inquest, had little to say about the outcome of the hearing, telling reporters he "would rather let the process unfold and let the people that actually do the policing have a look at that, and we'll wait for those comments down the road."
There are limitations to what a coroner's jury can do, Piche said.

"As good as some of the recommendations are, I think we have to be quite frank: where are they going to go?" he asked. "They may sit on a shelf somewhere in Regina, and that'll be the end of it. And it may be that a year from now, maybe two years from now, we're going to be discussing the very same thing."

Piche echoed comments Kovatch made to the jury before they began their deliberations, pointing out that one of the most important functions of an inquest is to provide a public airing of the facts involved, rather than leaving people to speculate about what happened.
He applauded the suggestion that the RCMP recruit more aboriginal members, noting that such recommendations have been made before.

The level of mistrust many aboriginal people feel toward police was graphically demonstrated at the start of the inquest, when so many aboriginal jury prospects excused themselves and admitted they could not be objective about the RCMP -- and that level of mistrust does not help efforts to recruit native people into the RCMP, he said.
Though it will likely never be known what went on inside the jury room, Piche said he was willing to bet the jury's view of the case "would very much have been divided on race lines.
